items.title: Under the Wave off Kanagawa (The Great Wave)
items.alt_neutral: Colour woodblock print: a towering clawed wave curls over three long rowing boats; a small snow-capped peak sits low in the distance; inscribed cartouche at upper left
items.caption: Colour print of a curling wave above three boats

made.note: Published and printed in Edo, today's Tokyo

journey_fact.text: Published in Edo c. 1829-33; how this impression left Japan is not documented. The Rijksmuseum bought it in 1956 with support from the Vereniging Rembrandt and the Dutch education ministry; seller not documented.

facts.text: It belongs to Hokusai's series Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji; Mount Fuji sits small in the background, dwarfed by the breaking wave.
It is a colour woodcut: the key block was printed in blue, with separate blocks for the other colours.

photo.author: Rijksmuseum
photo.pd_basis: Katsushika Hokusai died 1849; print published 1829-1833

items.title: Las Meninas
items.alt_neutral: Large oil painting: a small girl in a wide pale dress is attended by young women in a tall dim room; a painter stands at a huge canvas at left, a dog lies at right, a man pauses in a lit doorway at the back and two faces show in a mirror
items.caption: Painting of a girl, attendants, a painter and a dog

made.note: Painted in the Alcázar palace in Madrid, the room it shows

journey_fact.text: Royal Collection throughout: listed in the Alcázar of Madrid in 1700, then in the new Royal Palace, Madrid (1747-1818); entered the Prado in 1819.

facts.text: The king and queen, Philip IV and Mariana of Austria, appear only as reflections in the mirror on the back wall, watching the scene.
In 1724 Antonio Palomino gave it a section of its own in his history of Spanish painters, the only work he treated that way.

photo.author: Museo del Prado (Prado in Google Earth), via Wikimedia Commons
photo.pd_basis: Artist died 1660; Commons tags PD-Art (PD-old-auto-expired)

items.title: Lady with an Ermine
items.alt_neutral: Oil painting on panel: a young woman in a red and blue dress, with a fine band across her brow, turns her head to the side while cradling a slender white animal; black background with two lines of painted lettering at upper left
items.caption: Portrait of a young woman holding a white animal

kept.museum: Princes Czartoryski Museum, National Museum in Kraków

made.note: Painted at the court of Ludovico Sforza in Milan

journey_fact.text: Bought in Italy c. 1800 by Adam Jerzy Czartoryski (where and from whom is not documented); shown at Puławy from 1809; taken to Paris after 1831; in Kraków from 1882. Looted by the Nazis in 1939; back in Kraków 1946.

facts.text: The lettering 'LA BELE FERONIERE / LEONARD D'AWINCI' was added at Puławy, when the sitter was mistaken for a mistress of King Francis I of France.
The ermine alludes to Duke Ludovico Sforza. He received the Order of the Ermine in 1488 and was nicknamed 'Ermellino'.

photo.author: National Museum in Kraków
photo.pd_basis: Leonardo da Vinci died 1519; the MNK record's copyright field reads 'CC0 – Public domain'
photo.crop_note: Uncropped: the painted lettering at upper left is part of the paint surface.

items.title: The Temple of Dendur
items.alt_neutral: Sandstone shrine with a flat roofline: two columns with flower-shaped capitals frame an open porch and a doorway beyond; walls carved with rows of standing and seated figures; winged disk over the entrance
items.caption: Carved stone doorway framed by two columns

made.note: Built at Dendur in Nubia, a site now under Lake Nasser

when.label: built about 15 B.C.; completed by 10 B.C. or 10 CE (the Met gives both)
when.note: The Met's record gives both 10 B.C. and 10 CE for its completion, so any year from 15 BCE to 10 CE scores full marks.

journey_fact.text: Built at Dendur in Lower Nubia. With the Aswan High Dam reservoir set to flood the site in the 1960s, Egypt gave the temple to the United States in 1965; the US government awarded it to the Met in 1967.

facts.text: The 'pharaoh' carved on its walls is Rome's emperor Augustus, shown in traditional Egyptian regalia making offerings to the gods.
It honored the goddess Isis and, beside her, Pedesi and Pihor, deified sons of a local Nubian ruler.

photo.author: The Metropolitan Museum of Art
photo.pd_basis: Ancient temple of the reign of Augustus; Met API isPublicDomain=true, Met Open Access image (CC0)
photo.crop_note: Cropped to the temple: potted palms, a display box and the ceiling removed.

conflicts: Date: the Met's date line reads "completed by 10 CE", its numeric date fields give 10 BCE, and its description says "built about 15 B.C."; Wikidata gives c. 15 BCE. Scored with full marks for 15 BCE-10 CE, covering every date the Met gives.

items.title: A Sunday on La Grande Jatte — 1884
items.alt_neutral: Large painting built from tiny dots of colour: people in top hats, bustles and parasols stroll, sit and recline on a sunny riverside lawn; sailboats on the water; a small monkey on a leash at right
items.caption: Dotted painting of people on a sunny river bank

made.note: The museum names only France; the scene is an island near Paris

journey_fact.text: Kept by Seurat's family after his death in 1891; sold in 1900 to Casimir Brû; later with Lucie and Edmond Cousturier; sold in 1924 to Frederic Clay and Helen Birch Bartlett of Chicago; entered the Art Institute in 1926 as a memorial gift.

facts.text: Seurat laid tiny dabs of contrasting colour side by side (Pointillism), believing viewers' eyes would blend them into brighter hues.
Seurat returned to the canvas two years after starting it, adding figures such as the leashed monkey; the painted border came in 1888–89.

photo.author: Art Institute of Chicago
photo.pd_basis: Georges Seurat died 1891 (>70 years); faithful photo of a 2D work (PD-Art); AIC API is_public_domain=true

items.title: Mihrab (prayer niche) from the Madrasa Imami
items.alt_neutral: Tall tiled wall niche with a pointed arch, built from tiny cut tiles in deep blue, white and turquoise; bands of flowing and angular script frame the arch and a panel at the centre
items.caption: Tiled niche with a pointed arch and bands of script

journey_fact.text: Removed from the Madrasa Imami, Isfahan, in the late 1920s; by whom and under what permit is not documented. Shipped to Philadelphia, shown in London in 1931, with dealer A. Rabenou by 1931–39; bought for the Met in 1939.

facts.text: Made of glazed tiles cut to shape and set in mortar, it is, in the Met's words, one of the earliest and finest surviving examples of mosaic tile work.
Before the Met bought it, it was shown at the 1931 International Exhibition of Persian Art at Burlington House, London.

photo.author: The Metropolitan Museum of Art
photo.pd_basis: Work of 1354–55; Met API isPublicDomain=true, Met Open Access image (CC0)

items.title: Red-figure chous (wine jug)
items.alt_neutral: Rounded black ceramic jug with a three-lobed mouth; a frieze of three crouching nude youths wearing wreaths, painted in reddish-orange, play a game on the ground between egg-pattern borders; a crack crosses the shoulder
items.caption: Black jug painted with three crouching figures

kept.museum: J. Paul Getty Museum, Getty Villa

made.note: Made in Athens; found at Vulci, an Etruscan site in Italy

journey_fact.text: Found at Vulci, Italy (find date not documented); with Bonifacio Falcioni, Viterbo, by 1876. Tyszkiewicz sale, Paris, 1898; Béhague collection and heirs until Sotheby's Monaco 1987; Fleischman collection 1989; sold to the Getty 1996.

facts.text: A chous was used at the Anthesteria, a three-day Athenian festival for Dionysos; on its second day a drinking contest used these jugs to hold a standard amount of wine.
Its find spot, the Etruscan site of Vulci, suggests the jug was exported from Athens in antiquity.

photo.author: J. Paul Getty Museum
photo.pd_basis: Ancient Greek vase, c. 420 BCE; no copyright in the object.

conflicts: Date: the current Getty record gives about 420 B.C.; an older Getty catalogue (A Passion for Antiquities, 1994, cat. no. 42) dates it c. 440-430 BCE. The current museum record is used.

items.title: Jar with scenes of a scholar-official's life
items.alt_neutral: Porcelain jar painted deep blue on white: panels show a pavilion with a seated figure, gnarled pines, attendants and playing children; set on a carved dark-wood stand
items.caption: Blue-and-white jar painted with buildings, trees and figures

journey_fact.text: Made at the Jingdezhen kilns in 1522-66; how it left China is not documented. It is recorded in the Magrath Collection (date not documented), then with Worcester R. Warner of Cleveland, who gave it to the museum in 1917.

facts.text: Its painted scenes follow a scholar-official through the four seasons, from leaving home for the civil service exams to writing in old age.
It bears the reign mark 'Da Ming Jiajing nian zhi': made in the Ming dynasty, Jiajing period.

photo.author: Cleveland Museum of Art
photo.pd_basis: Anonymous porcelain made 1522-1566

items.title: Shiva Nataraja, Lord of the Dance
items.alt_neutral: Dark bronze statue: a four-armed figure dances on one leg inside a ring of flames, hair fanning out to both sides, one foot on a small crouching figure; stepped pedestal
items.caption: Metal statue of a four-armed figure inside a ring of flames

kept.museum: Rijksmuseum (on loan from the Royal Asian Art Society)

journey_fact.text: Made in Tamil Nadu c. 1100-1200; how and when it left India is not documented. Dealer C.T. Loo, Paris, sold it in 1935 to the Royal Asian Art Society, which has lent it to the Rijksmuseum since 1972.

facts.text: Museum research suggests it was worshipped only briefly, then buried at an unknown site in India, and reached the art market in the early 20th century without major restoration.
The bronze stands 153 cm high and weighs 255 kg; its separate pedestal adds another 40 kg.

photo.author: Rijksmuseum
photo.pd_basis: Anonymous bronze of c. 1100-1200

items.title: Boulevard Montmartre, morning, cloudy weather
items.alt_neutral: Oil painting seen from a high window: a long tree-lined boulevard in grey morning light, crowded with horse-drawn carriages and walkers between rows of tall pale apartment blocks
items.caption: Painting of a busy tree-lined street seen from above

journey_fact.text: Painted in Paris in 1897. Dealer Durand-Ruel bought it at a London Guildhall show in 1898; he lent it to London's Grafton Gallery in 1905, where Bernard Hall bought it for Melbourne's Felton Bequest.

facts.text: One of 14 views of the Boulevard Montmartre that Pissarro painted from a hotel-room window between 10 February and 17 April 1897.
Its 1905 purchase made the NGV one of the first public galleries in the world to acquire a French Impressionist painting.

photo.author: National Gallery of Victoria (Google Art Project), via Wikimedia Commons
photo.pd_basis: Camille Pissarro died 1903; faithful photo of a 2D work

items.title: The Night Watch
items.alt_neutral: Very large oil painting: a crowd of armed men with pikes, muskets, a banner and a drum spill out of a dark archway; a man in black with a red sash and one in pale gold stride forward at centre, a small girl in gold glows at left
items.caption: Painting of a crowd with pikes, muskets and a drum

kept.museum: Rijksmuseum (on loan from the City of Amsterdam)

journey_fact.text: Painted for the Kloveniersdoelen guild hall; moved to the Town Hall on Dam square in 1715 and to the Trippenhuis in 1808; on loan to the museum from the City of Amsterdam since 1808.

facts.text: Painted for the great hall of the Kloveniersdoelen, headquarters of Amsterdam's arquebusiers' civic guard.
Its nickname 'The Night Watch' only dates from the end of the 18th century; it shows the company of Captain Frans Banninck Cocq.

photo.author: Rijksmuseum
photo.pd_basis: Artist died 1669; Rijksmuseum record 'Copyright: Public domain', and the linked-art VisualItem carries the Public Domain Mark 1.0

items.title: Statuette of a Nike
items.alt_neutral: Small painted clay statuette of a young woman in a thin, high-belted dress, striding forward with one arm raised (hand broken off) and the other held out; worn traces of pink and orange paint; set on a small white mount
items.caption: Clay figure in a flowing dress with one arm raised

journey_fact.text: Owned by the 6th Earl of Harewood (d. 1947); sold at Christie's, London, 1951, to Spink & Son, who sold it to J. Paul Getty. He gave it to the Getty Museum in 1970. Find spot and how it left Turkey are not documented.

facts.text: The figure shows Nike, goddess of victory, alighting; the soles of her sandals and traces of painted straps are still visible.

photo.author: J. Paul Getty Museum (Open Content Program; photographer not named)
photo.pd_basis: Hellenistic terracotta, 3rd century BCE; no copyright in the object.

conflicts: Getty API begin/end = -249/-200, which looks like astronomical year numbering; the label 'second half of 3rd century B.C.' converts to -250..-201 under the content guide's date rule. Used -250..-201.
Object is in Getty storage per the record (Villa Collection); kept coordinates use the Getty Villa building.
No Wikidata item found for this object.

items.title: Royal Carpet with Silk and Metal Thread
items.alt_neutral: Knotted silk carpet hung on a wall: salmon-orange and green borders around a grey-lilac field of mirrored scrolling arabesques and blossoms, with long fringes at top and bottom
items.caption: Fringed textile with floral patterns and orange and green borders

journey_fact.text: Made in Isfahan; how and when it reached Europe is not documented. CMA lists it as formerly in an Austrian abbey (Chorherrenstift 'Voran'), then with dealer Mario Veneziani, Rome, who sold it to the museum in 1926.

facts.text: Persian carpets with silk and metal thread were long miscalled 'Polish' after one appeared in the Polish exhibit at the 1878 Paris World's Fair.
Safavid royal workshops wove luxurious silks like this for the court and also for export to European aristocrats.

photo.author: Cleveland Museum of Art
photo.pd_basis: Work of 1600–1625; CMA share_license_status = CC0

conflicts: CMA provenance spells 'Chorherrenstift Voran, Austria'; this is presumably Stift Vorau (Augustinian canons, Styria; Wikidata Q770954) - my inference, the CMA record does not say Vorau.
Wikidata Q80000690: P1071 Isfahan, P195 CMA (agree); no P571.

items.title: Tibor chocolatero (Chocolate jar)
items.alt_neutral: Tin-glazed earthenware jar painted dark blue on cream: birds and leafy scrolls in panels, swags at the shoulder; a hinged iron lid with a key standing on top
items.caption: Glazed earthenware jar painted blue on cream, with a locked iron lid

journey_fact.text: Earlier history not documented. Owned in Mexico City by Herbert Pickering Lewis (d. 1922); his widow Eva Lewis exported it from Mexico in Oct-Nov 1923 and gave it to the Art Institute of Chicago that December.

facts.text: Its iron cover, collar and lock suggest it held something valuable, such as cacao beans.
Talavera poblana likely takes its name from Talavera de la Reina in Spain; its blue-and-white designs also show Chinese influence.

photo.author: Art Institute of Chicago
photo.pd_basis: Anonymous ceramic made 1725-1775

conflicts: Wikidata Q111723325 inception is 1700 at decade precision (1700s); museum says 1725-75
Wikidata location of creation points to Q1029938 'Puebla, Mexico', a disambiguation page with no coordinates; this record uses the city Q125293 (Heroica Puebla de Zaragoza)

items.title: Sunflowers
items.alt_neutral: Thickly painted oil on canvas: a bunch of large yellow flowers, some in full bloom and some wilting and turning to seed, fills a round earthenware vase on a narrow ochre ledge against a pale yellow wall; a thin blue line runs along the ledge
items.caption: Painting of large yellow flowers in a round vase

made.note: Painted at the Yellow House, his rented home in Arles

journey_fact.text: How it left Arles is not documented. Later owned by the artist's sister-in-law Jo van Gogh-Bonger, then her son until 1923; sold by the Leicester Galleries, London, to the Courtauld Fund in 1924; moved from the Tate in 1961.

facts.text: Van Gogh painted his first four versions in one week of August 1888 at the Yellow House, his rented home in Arles, to decorate it for Paul Gauguin's visit.
This and the Munich version are the most important of the seven; Van Gogh signed both 'Vincent' and chose them for an exhibition in Brussels in 1889.

photo.author: The National Gallery, London (online catalogue), via Wikimedia Commons
photo.pd_basis: Vincent van Gogh died 1890; Commons tags the file PD-Art (PD-old-100-expired)
photo.crop_note: Uncropped: the signature on the vase is part of the paint surface.

items.title: Girl with a Pearl Earring
items.alt_neutral: Oil painting of a young woman against a dark background, glancing back over her shoulder with lips parted; a blue and yellow cloth is wound into a turban on her head, a large glinting drop hangs from her ear, and a white collar shows above an ochre jacket
items.caption: Painting of a young woman in a turban looking over her shoulder

made.note: Vermeer lived and worked in Delft all his life

journey_fact.text: Possibly owned by Delft collector Pieter van Ruijven and heirs, and sold in Amsterdam in 1696; 1696-1881 not documented. Bought at a Hague auction in 1881 by A.A. des Tombe for 2.30 guilders; his bequest to the Mauritshuis, 1903.

facts.text: It is not a portrait but a tronie: a study of an imaginary figure, here a girl in exotic dress with an oriental turban and an improbably large pearl.
Vermeer lived and worked in Delft all his life; the Delft collector Pieter van Ruijven owned about half of the paintings Vermeer ever produced.

photo.author: Mauritshuis, The Hague, via Wikimedia Commons
photo.pd_basis: Johannes Vermeer died 1675; Commons tags the file PD-Art (PD-old-auto-expired)

items.title: The Kiss (Lovers)
items.alt_neutral: Square painting glittering with gold leaf: a man in a robe patterned with black and white rectangles bends to embrace a kneeling woman in a robe of coloured circles, his face pressed to her cheek, at the edge of a flowery meadow before a gold-flecked background
items.caption: Gold-leaf painting of an embracing couple on a flowery meadow

made.note: Shown unfinished in Vienna in 1908, then finished in Klimt's studio

when.label: c. 1907–1909
when.note: Begun probably in 1907, shown unfinished in 1908, and reworked until about the end of June 1909

journey_fact.text: Shown as 'Lovers' at the Kunstschau Wien in 1908 and bought by the ministry for the Moderne Galerie, now the Belvedere, which received it in July 1909 once Klimt had finished it. Evacuated outside Vienna in the Second World War.

facts.text: Klimt used real gold, silver and platinum leaf; the Belvedere says he painted it at the height of his Golden Period, without a direct commission.
A photo taken at the 1908 show records unpainted patches at lower left; Klimt took it back to his studio and probably finished reworking it by the end of June 1909.

photo.author: Belvedere, Vienna (Google Art Project), via Wikimedia Commons
photo.pd_basis: Gustav Klimt died 1918; Commons tags the file PD-Art (PD-old-100-expired)
photo.crop_note: Uncropped: the signature at lower right is part of the paint surface.

conflicts: Date: the Belvedere record gives c. 1907–1909; Wikidata Q698487 P571 gives 1907 with earliest 1907 and latest 1908. The museum record is used.

items.title: The Girls on the Bridge
items.alt_neutral: Oil painting: three young figures in white, red and green dresses, one in a straw hat, lean on a wooden railing with their backs to us, looking down at dark water; a pale road curves away past white houses, a huge round dark-green tree and a small yellow moon
items.caption: Painting of three figures in bright dresses at a railing by water

made.note: Munch wrote that he painted it in Åsgårdstrand, the town it shows

when.label: Antagelig 1901 (probably 1901)
when.note: The museum dates it 'probably 1901'; Munch wrote that he painted it in the summer of 1901

journey_fact.text: Shown in Kristiania (now Oslo) in 1901 and at the Berlin Secession in 1902. Collector Olaf Schou gave it to the National Gallery, now part of the Nasjonalmuseet, in 1909; how Schou acquired it is not documented.

facts.text: Munch wrote that he painted it in Åsgårdstrand in the summer of 1901; he had bought a small house in the coastal town in 1898 and used local people as models.
It was first shown in 1901 as 'Summer Evening'; the museum's canvas is the first of several versions Munch painted of the motif.

photo.author: Nasjonalmuseet / Børre Høstland
photo.pd_basis: Edvard Munch died 1944 (more than 70 years); the museum marks the work 'Free use – no known copyright restrictions'
photo.crop_note: Uncropped: the initials at lower left are part of the paint surface.

items.title: The Birth of Venus
items.alt_neutral: Wide painting on canvas: a nude woman with long, flowing reddish-gold hair stands on a giant scallop shell drifting to the shore; at left two winged figures, entwined, blow her in among falling roses; at right a woman in a flowered white dress holds out a pink cloak beside a row of trees
items.caption: Painting of a nude woman on a giant shell blown ashore by winds

made.note: First recorded at the Medici villa of Castello, in Florence

journey_fact.text: Described by Vasari at the Medici villa of Castello, Florence, and listed in its inventory in 1598; later held in the Guardaroba (wardrobe) in Florence until 1815, when it entered the Uffizi.

facts.text: Orange trees, a Medici emblem (the fruit was then called 'mala medica'), support the view that a member of the Medici family commissioned it.
Unlike the Primavera, painted on wood, it is on canvas, a support widely used in the 15th century for decorative works for noble houses.

photo.author: Gallerie degli Uffizi (Google Art Project), via Wikimedia Commons
photo.pd_basis: Artist died 1510; Commons tags PD-Art (PD-old-100-expired)

items.title: The Starry Night
items.alt_neutral: Oil painting in thick, swirling strokes: a deep blue sky churns with spirals, glowing yellow orbs and a bright crescent moon above a small village with a pointed steeple at the foot of rolling hills; a tall, dark, flame-like tree rises in the left foreground
items.caption: Painting of a swirling sky with glowing orbs over a small village

made.note: Painted in Saint-Rémy, where he spent 1889-90 at the Saint-Paul asylum

journey_fact.text: Kept by van Gogh until Sept 1889, then his brother Theo, Paris; Jo van Gogh-Bonger, Amsterdam, from 1891; Leclercq and Schuffenecker, Paris, 1900-05; Georgette van Stolk, Rotterdam, 1906-38; Paul Rosenberg; MoMA by exchange, 1941.

facts.text: Inspired by the view from his window at the Saint-Paul-de-Mausole asylum in Saint-Rémy; the village came from other views, as it could not be seen from that window.
Although it shows the night sky, van Gogh painted it in several sessions during the day, in mid-June 1889.

photo.author: Google Art Project, via Wikimedia Commons
photo.pd_basis: Artist died 1890; Commons tags PD-Art (PD-old-100-expired)

items.title: Wanderer above the Sea of Fog
items.alt_neutral: Upright oil painting: a man in a dark green coat, seen from behind and holding a walking stick, stands on a rocky crag and looks out over banks of mist from which jagged rocks, peaks and distant hills emerge under a pale, cloudy sky
items.caption: Painting of a man seen from behind on a rock above drifting mist

kept.museum: Hamburger Kunsthalle (on permanent loan from the Stiftung Hamburger Kunstsammlungen)

made.note: Shows peaks he sketched on walks; composed in his studio in Dresden

when.label: um 1817 (c. 1817)
when.note: The Kunsthalle notes that the work is neither signed nor dated and that its dating is not secure.

journey_fact.text: Owners from Friedrich to 1938 not documented. Berlin dealer W. A. Luz had it by July 1938 and sold it to Ernst Henke, Essen; Allied custody 1945-48; Bielefeld private collection by 1957; bought 1970 by the Hamburg foundation that lends it.

facts.text: The rock under the figure comes from a drawing Friedrich made on 3 June 1813 in Saxon Switzerland; the cone-shaped peak at left draws on a study he made in Bohemia in May 1808.
Friedrich moved to Dresden around 1800 and explored its surroundings on foot; later, in his studio, he assembled such nature studies into this composition.

photo.author: Hamburger Kunsthalle (photo: Elke Walford), via Wikimedia Commons
photo.pd_basis: Artist died 1840; Commons tags PD-Art (PD-old-100-expired)

conflicts: Date: Wikidata P571 gives c. 1818; the Hamburger Kunsthalle record gives 'um 1817' (about 1817) and says the dating is not secure. The museum record is used.

Made: neither the Kunsthalle record nor Wikidata (no P1071) names the place of creation. Dresden is inferred from Kunsthalle texts: Friedrich settled in Dresden in 1798 (exhibition page), died there in 1840 (object record) and composed this picture in his studio from earlier sketches (Wanderer story).

items.title: The Assumption of the Virgin
items.alt_neutral: Very tall oil painting in two zones: below, bearded men in bright red, yellow, green and blue robes crowd around an empty stone tomb, gesturing upward; above, a woman in a red gown and blue mantle rises on a thin crescent moon among angels and clouds
items.caption: Tall painting of a woman rising on a crescent moon above a crowd

made.note: Painted for the high altar of a convent church in Toledo

journey_fact.text: In Santo Domingo el Antiguo, Toledo, from 1579; sold c. 1830 to Infante Sebastián Gabriel; seized by the state 1835, returned 1861; lent to the Prado 1902-04; bought 1904 by Durand-Ruel with Havemeyer funds; sold to the Art Institute 1906.

facts.text: It was the central image of El Greco's first major commission, the high altarpiece of the convent church of Santo Domingo el Antiguo in Toledo, ordered in 1577.
El Greco signed it in Greek on a painted slip of paper at lower right: 'Domenikos Theotokopoulos, Cretan, displayed this in 1577'.

photo.author: Art Institute of Chicago
photo.pd_basis: El Greco died 1614 (>70 years); faithful photo of a 2D work; AIC API is_public_domain=true

conflicts: Made: the AIC record's place field gives Greece, labelled 'Artist's nationality', not where it was painted; its provenance and text place the commission and installation in Toledo, which is used. Wikidata has no P1071.
Date: Wikidata P571 gives 1577 (the year in the signature); the AIC record gives 1577–79. The museum record is used.

items.title: The Golden Burial Mask of Tutankhamun
items.alt_neutral: Gold face mask of a young man with inlaid dark-rimmed eyes and brows, a long braided false beard and a headcloth striped in gold and deep blue; a rearing snake and a bird head rise from the brow; a broad collar of blue, red and turquoise bands covers the chest
items.caption: Gold mask with a striped headcloth, a braided beard and inlaid eyes

made.note: Found in the king's tomb at Luxor; the workshop that made it is not recorded

when.label: New Kingdom
when.note: The museum gives only the period (c. 1550-1070 BCE); the mask was made for Tutankhamun, who died about 1323 BCE.

journey_fact.text: From the tomb Howard Carter found in the Valley of the Kings, Luxor, in 1922; kept for nearly a century in the Egyptian Museum on Cairo's Tahrir Square, then moved to the Grand Egyptian Museum near Giza (transfer date not documented).

facts.text: It was found over the head and shoulders of Tutankhamun's mummy; it shows him as Osiris and as the sun god Re, whose body was gold and hair lapis lazuli.
It went on show at the centre of the Grand Egyptian Museum's Tutankhamun galleries in November 2025, with almost all of his tomb treasure displayed together for the first time.

photo.author: Dawid Wdowczyk, via Wikimedia Commons
photo.pd_basis: Ancient Egyptian funerary mask of the New Kingdom; no copyright in the object.

conflicts: Location: Wikidata P276 still gives the Egyptian Museum, Cairo (Q201219); the GEM record lists the mask in its Tutankhamun Galleries, on show there since November 2025 (AFP). The GEM is used.
Date: the GEM gives only 'New Kingdom'; Wikidata P571 gives c. 1323 BCE and 1334-1324 BCE. The range is the New Kingdom span from Wikidata Q180568 (c. 1550-1070 BCE).
Made: the GEM 'Provenance' names Upper Egypt, Luxor, the find site; Wikidata P1071 is Q180568 (the New Kingdom state). Made is set to Egypt at country level because the workshop is not recorded.

items.title: The Standard of Ur
items.alt_neutral: Long panel of pale shell and red stone figures set into a deep blue mosaic ground, in three rows: at the bottom four-wheeled chariots drawn by donkey-like animals ride over fallen men; in the middle cloaked soldiers march and drive naked captives; at the top a taller central figure faces a line of prisoners, a chariot waiting behind him
items.caption: Mosaic panel: rows of chariots, soldiers and captives on blue

made.note: Found in a royal tomb at Ur; the museum names no workshop

when.label: 2550 BC - 2400 BC (collection record); 2600–2400 BC (gallery page)
when.note: The museum's record gives 2550-2400 BC and its gallery page 2600-2400 BC; any year from 2600 to 2400 BCE scores full marks.

journey_fact.text: Excavated by Leonard Woolley in royal tomb PG 779 in the Royal Cemetery at Ur; came to the British Museum through a division of finds with Iraq's Department of Antiquities (registration number 1928,1010.3).

facts.text: Found crushed in a king's tomb looted in antiquity, between a man's shoulder and skull; its wooden box had rotted away and hundreds of inlay pieces had to be reassembled.
Woolley dug at Ur for a joint British Museum and Penn Museum expedition begun in 1922; of nearly 2,000 burials he found, he called sixteen "royal tombs".

photo.author: LeastCommonAncestor, from a photo by BabelStone (Andrew West), via Wikimedia Commons
photo.pd_basis: Sumerian object of about 2600-2400 BCE; no copyright in the object.

conflicts: Place: the British Museum names Ur only as the find spot (royal tomb PG 779) and records no place of making, so made is the region around it, Sumer (Wikidata Q35355, about 130 km from Ur), not the city.
Date: the collection record gives 2550-2400 BC, the Room 56 gallery page 2600-2400 BC, Wikidata P571 c. 2501 BCE. The range covers both museum dates.

items.title: Clay Figurine ("Dogū") with Goggle-Like Eyes
items.alt_neutral: Hollow dark grey clay figure with huge oval eyes each crossed by a slit, a tiny nose and mouth and a crown-shaped crest on the head; broad rounded shoulders, stubby arms, a narrow waist and wide hips; the body is covered in incised swirls and dotted raised bands; the left leg is missing
items.caption: Hollow clay figure with huge oval eyes and swirling incised patterns

made.note: Found at Kamegaoka in Tsugaru, Aomori; a type made in the Tōhoku region

journey_fact.text: Unearthed in 1887 in the boggy lowlands of the Kamegaoka site in Tsugaru, Aomori, where ritual dumps held many figurines; how and when it entered the Tokyo National Museum is not documented.

facts.text: Figurines of this kind, called shakōki dogū after snow goggles, belong to the Kamegaoka culture of the Tōhoku region in the Final Jōmon period; this is the best known of them.
The eyes were once thought to show snow goggles; they are now read as an exaggerated way of showing eyes. Traces of red suggest the whole figure was once painted red.

photo.author: Tokyo National Museum, via ColBase (resized)
photo.pd_basis: Prehistoric clay figure of 1000-400 BC; no copyright in the object.

conflicts: Made: the museum records only the find place (Tsugaru City, Aomori; ColBase's production-place field is empty) and Wikidata has no P1071; made is set to the Tōhoku region, where the museums' e-Museum places the Kamegaoka culture of this type.

items.title: Mochica portrait bottle of a figure in a turban
items.alt_neutral: Sculpted ceramic bottle in the shape of a human head with a calm, lifelike face in glossy red-brown, painted in three vertical bands; a cream headcloth frames the face and a band of red triangles crosses the brow; a hollow arched handle with one upright spout rises from the top
items.caption: Ceramic bottle shaped as a human head in a patterned headcloth

made.note: The museum records only the region: 'Costa Norte', Peru's north coast

when.label: Larco: Época Auge (1 dC - 800 dC); Rowe: Horizonte Medio (600 dC - 1000 dC)
when.note: The museum gives two chronologies, 1-800 CE (Larco) and 600-1000 CE (Rowe); any year from 1 to 1000 CE scores full marks.

journey_fact.text: Find spot and acquisition not documented. Rafael Larco Hoyle built the collection from 1923, buying many north-coast collections, founded the museum at Hacienda Chiclín in 1926 and moved it to Lima in the 1950s.

facts.text: The museum's founder, Rafael Larco Hoyle, proposed the first chronological order of north-coast cultures in 1946, before radiocarbon dating was developed.
Larco Hoyle gathered about 50,000 pieces, buying collections from the Chicama, Moche, Virú and Santa valleys of the north coast.

photo.author: Pierre André Leclercq, via Wikimedia Commons
photo.pd_basis: Mochica ceramic of 1-1000 CE; no copyright in the object.

conflicts: Date: the record gives two chronologies, Larco 'Época Auge' (1-800 CE) and Rowe 'Horizonte Medio' (600-1000 CE); the range covers both. The Commons file page gives 1-800 CE.

Made: the record names only 'Región: Costa Norte'. Wikidata has no place item for Peru's north coast except the travel region Q14204197 'Northern Coast (Peru)' (Tumbes to Ancash), whose coordinates are used.
No Wikidata item for this object; the Commons file names accession ML000174 and links the Larco record.

items.title: Along the River During the Qingming Festival
items.alt_neutral: Long painting in muted browns: a crowd pours over a high arched wooden bridge above a wide stream; below it a big boat with oarsmen swings toward the arch while others watch; tiled roofs, stalls, carts and parasols crowd the banks
items.caption: Painting of a crowded arched bridge over water with boats

made.note: Shows the Song capital, today Kaifeng, where its painter studied

when.label: Northern Song dynasty, 12th century
when.note: The museum dates it Northern Song (ended 1127) and says it re-creates 12th-century life in the capital: 1101-1127.

journey_fact.text: Its route from the Northern Song capital to the Qing court is not documented here. Puyi, the last emperor, took it with him when he left the Forbidden City in 1924; it was recovered in 1945 and kept at the Palace Museum.

facts.text: The museum says it shows the Northern Song capital Bianjing, today Kaifeng, at the Qingming festival: the Bian river, the arched Rainbow Bridge and an east city gate.
The earliest attribution to Zhang Zeduan is a colophon dated 1186 by the Jin court curator Zhang Zhu; it calls him a Hanlin academician who had studied in the capital.

photo.author: Unknown photographer (scan via Baidu Tieba), via Wikimedia Commons
photo.pd_basis: Northern Song painting, 12th century; Commons tags the file PD-Art (PD-old-100) as a faithful reproduction of the Palace Museum original
photo.crop_note: The Commons file is already a detail of the scroll (the arched bridge); the full scroll is about 21 times wider than tall

conflicts: Place: the Palace Museum object record names no place of making; it says the scroll shows the Northern Song capital Bianjing (today Kaifeng, Henan). Henan rests on the museum's own artist biography (Minghuaji: Zhang Zeduan studied in the capital as a young man) and its Northern Song date, when the capital was Kaifeng. Region level, not city. Wikidata Q714802 has no P1071.

Date: the museum's text says Northern Song (北宋) and that the scroll re-creates 12th-century life in the capital; its digital catalogue lists the period only as Song (宋). Scored 1101-1127. Wikidata P571 gives 1085; Wikipedia notes scholars disagree whether it was painted before or after the fall of the Northern Song in 1127.
Wikidata P195 (The Palace Museum) agrees with the museum.

items.title: Portable Altar of Countess Gertrude
items.alt_neutral: Small rectangular box covered in gold: seven haloed standing figures in relief under enamelled arches line the long side; bands set with coloured stones and pearls frame them; a speckled reddish stone slab forms the top
items.caption: Gold box with standing figures under arches and set gems

made.note: The museum gives Lower Saxony with a question mark; made for a countess of Brunswick

when.label: c. 1045
when.note: The museum dates it c. 1045 and gives 1040-1050 as its date range.

journey_fact.text: In the treasury of Brunswick's Cathedral of St. Blaise from about 1045, then owned by the House of Brunswick-Lüneburg (dates not documented); sold by Goldschmidt Galleries, New York, to the museum in 1931.

facts.text: Countess Gertrude of Brunswick commissioned it; the Latin inscription round the stone says Gertrude offers to Christ this stone that glistens with gems and gold.
Its porphyry altar stone, an imperial colour used only by the imperial family, signals Gertrude's claim of imperial lineage for her own dynasty.

photo.author: Cleveland Museum of Art
photo.pd_basis: Anonymous metalwork of c. 1045; CMA share_license_status = CC0

conflicts: Place: the museum writes 'Germany, Lower Saxony?', with a question mark; its description says Countess Gertrude of Brunswick commissioned it. Wikidata Q60779219 has no P1071.
Date: museum c. 1045 (date range 1040-1050); Wikidata P571 c. 1045 agrees. English Wikipedia's Guelph Treasure article captions it 'shortly after 1038'.
Wikidata P195 (Cleveland Museum of Art) agrees with the museum.

items.title: Portrait of a Halberdier (Francesco Guardi?)
items.alt_neutral: Oil painting of a youth seen to the thighs, in a puffed cream doublet with a fine gold chain, a red cap with a gold badge and red hose; he grips a tall wooden pole and rests one hand on his hip beside a sword hilt; dark green wall behind
items.caption: Painting of a youth in a red cap holding a tall pole

made.note: Getty lists Italy; its text ties it to Vasari's portrait made in the siege of Florence

journey_fact.text: Riccardi family, Florence, by 1612; how it left Italy is not documented. Lebrun sale, Paris, 1810, to Cardinal Fesch; Fesch sale, Rome, 1845; Princess Mathilde sale, Paris, 1904; Stillman family; Christie's, New York, 1989, to the Getty.

facts.text: Vasari wrote that during the siege of Florence, about 1529, Pontormo painted the young nobleman Francesco Guardi as a soldier; a Guardi boy was born in 1514.
Auctioned to the Getty in May 1989 for 32.5 million dollars, then the highest price ever paid for an old master painting.

photo.author: J. Paul Getty Museum (Open Content Program)
photo.pd_basis: Pontormo died 1557; Getty rights statement 'No Copyright'; IIIF manifest rights CC0 1.0

conflicts: Place: the Getty's creation-place field gives only Italy; its description cites Vasari, who says Pontormo painted this sitter, Francesco Guardi, as a soldier during the siege of Florence (about 1529). Florence is used. Wikidata Q3607621 has no P1071.
Date: Getty 1529–1530; Wikidata P571 gives 1529. Those who see the sitter as the young Cosimo I de' Medici date it to 1537 (Wikipedia); the Getty mentions the Cosimo suggestion but keeps 1529–1530.
The Getty record gives the painting's current location as Storage; kept coordinates are the Getty Center (Wikidata P276, same as the museum's P625).

items.title: The Code of Hammurabi
items.alt_neutral: Tall polished dark stone slab with a rounded top, on a dark ground: a carved relief at the top shows a standing figure, one hand raised to the mouth, facing a seated figure on a stepped throne who holds out a rod and ring; dense columns of tiny carved signs cover the rest
items.caption: Tall stone slab: a carved scene above dense columns of writing

made.note: The Louvre names Iraq = Mesopotamia; found at Susa, Iran, taken there as war spoil

when.label: 1792–1750 BC (1st dynasty of Babylon: Hammurabi)
when.note: The Louvre dates it to Hammurabi's reign; its gallery text says the laws were engraved around 1750 BC.

journey_fact.text: Carried to Susa, Iran, as war spoil by the Elamite king Shutruk-Nahhunte (reigned about 1185–1160 BC); found there by French excavators in 1902 and on display at the Louvre since 1904.

facts.text: It records 282 legal judgements handed down by Hammurabi, king of Babylon, on family, property, trade and labour; the text was engraved around 1750 BC.
The Louvre records it as acquired through the division of finds from Jacques de Morgan's French excavations at Susa; it is owned by the French State.

photo.author: Mbzt, via Wikimedia Commons
photo.pd_basis: Ancient stele of 1792–1750 BC; no copyright in the object

conflicts: Place: the Louvre names only 'Irak = Mésopotamie' (Wikidata P1071 Mesopotamia agrees). The text's epilogue says it was set up in the Esagila temple at Babylon (L. W. King translation, Avalon Project); Martha Roth suggests this stele was taken from Sippar (Wikipedia). Neither city is in the Louvre record.
Date: the Louvre gives -1792/-1750 (Hammurabi's reign); Wikidata P571 gives c. 1793 BCE, earliest -1793, latest -1751, one year off, probably a year-numbering difference. The Louvre is used.
Discovery: the Louvre record gives 1901-1902; its gallery page says 1902. Wikidata P195 (Louvre, Department of Near Eastern Antiquities) agrees.

items.title: Washington Crossing the Delaware
items.alt_neutral: Very wide oil painting: a tall man in a cloak and three-cornered hat stands in the bow of a crowded wooden boat while men row and pole it through floating ice; behind him a man holds up a big wind-torn flag with stars; more boats, soldiers and horses follow under a stormy dawn sky
items.caption: Oil painting of soldiers rowing a boat through ice under a flag

made.note: Signed 'E. Leutze / Dusseldorf 1851'; it shows a winter river crossing of 1776

journey_fact.text: Signed in Düsseldorf in 1851; with the dealers Goupil, Vibert and Company, Paris and New York, 1851-52; owned by Marshall O. Roberts, New York, 1852-80; sold at auction in 1897 to John S. Kennedy, who gave it to the Met that year.

facts.text: The Met says it was a great success in Leutze's native Germany, then in revolutionary fervour, and in the United States, where it quickly became an iconic image.
It hangs in a reproduction of its original trophy-style frame, rebuilt from a photograph by Mathew B. Brady.

photo.author: The Metropolitan Museum of Art
photo.pd_basis: Emanuel Leutze died in 1868; painted 1851. Met Open Access API isPublicDomain: true.
photo.crop_note: 1% trimmed from each edge to remove the thin black border of the Met file

conflicts: Made: the Met record names no 'made in' field; the place comes from its Signatures field ('E. Leutze / Dusseldorf 1851'). The Met's Culture field says 'American' and Wikidata P495 (country of origin) says United States; Wikidata has no P1071.
Wikidata P195 (Met, from 1897, inv. 97.34) and P571 (1851) agree with the Met.

items.title: Ginevra de' Benci
items.alt_neutral: Small, almost square oil painting on wood: a pale young woman with tight auburn curls and heavy-lidded eyes, in a brown dress laced with blue, faces the viewer before a dark bush of spiky needles; at right a misty river landscape with slim trees and a distant spire
items.caption: Oil portrait of a pale young woman before a spiky dark bush

made.note: The gallery calls it one of the first portraits made in Florence with an outdoor setting

journey_fact.text: Presumably bought in Florence by Prince Johann Adam I of Liechtenstein before 1712 (not documented); in the Liechtenstein collection, Vienna, by 1733; taken to Vaduz in WWII; bought by the National Gallery of Art in February 1967.

facts.text: The spiky juniper bush behind her is a pun on her name: ginepro is the Italian word for juniper.
About six inches were cut off the bottom of the panel at some point; the original probably showed her waist and hands. Leonardo's fingerprint is visible where the sky meets the juniper.

photo.author: National Gallery of Art, Washington
photo.pd_basis: Leonardo da Vinci died in 1519. NGA open data published_images.csv lists this primary image with openaccess=1 (NGA Open Access images are CC0).
photo.crop_note: Shows the original panel only, without the strip added later at the bottom

conflicts: Made: the NGA object record gives no place of execution (school 'Florentine'; provenance 'presumably purchased in Florence'); Florence comes from the NGA's own publication 'An Eye for Art: Leonardo da Vinci'. Wikidata has no P1071.

Journey: the NGA record says presumably bought by Prince Johann Adam Andreas I before 1712; the same NGA publication says 'it is believed Prince Carl Eusebius of Liechtenstein purchased this painting after 1611'. The record is used.

items.title: Bust of Queen Nefertiti
items.alt_neutral: Painted stone bust of a woman with a long slender neck, full red lips and dark-lined eyes, one eye inlaid and the other an empty socket; she wears a tall flat-topped blue headdress bound by a coloured band, and a broad painted collar of floral bands covers the shoulders
items.caption: Painted stone bust: a woman in a tall flat-topped blue headdress

made.note: Found in 1912 in the sculptor Thutmose's workshop at Amarna

when.label: ca. 1351–1334 BC
when.note: The museum dates it to Akhenaten's reign, ca. 1351–1334 BC; its overview page says it was created around 1340 BC.

journey_fact.text: Dug up on 6 December 1912 in workshop P 47.2 at Amarna by Ludwig Borchardt's team; given to the German share in the January 1913 division of finds, it went to the dig's funder James Simon, who gave it to the museum in 1920.

facts.text: The right eye is black-dyed beeswax under a polished rock-crystal cornea; the left was never inlaid, Borchardt concluded, a view the museum says is now debated.
Borchardt's excavation diary on the day of the find: "Work absolutely exceptional. Description is useless, must be seen."

photo.author: Philip Pikart, via Wikimedia Commons
photo.pd_basis: Ancient Egyptian sculpture of ca. 1351–1334 BC; no copyright in the object.

conflicts: Date: the museum gives ca. 1351–1334 BC (record: reign of Amenhotep IV / Akhenaten); Wikidata P571 gives c. 1350 BCE, earliest 1353, latest 1336 BCE. The museum range is used.

Place: the SMB object record names only the find spot 'P 47.02'; the museum's own bust pages name Egypt, Tell el-Amarna, house P 47.2, the workshop complex attributed to the sculptor Thutmose. Wikidata has no P1071 (P189 find location: Amarna).

claimant_source.text: Zahi Hawass, Egypt's former antiquities minister, petitions for its return, saying records show it "was removed from Egypt against the letter and the spirit of the Egyptian laws in effect at the time".

items.title: Return of the Prodigal Son
items.alt_neutral: Large dark oil painting: a ragged young man with a shaven head kneels with his back to us, one shoe slipped off his bare foot, while an old man in a red cloak bends over him and lays both hands on his shoulders; a tall man in red and other figures watch from the shadows
items.caption: Painting: a kneeling man in rags embraced by an old man in red

made.note: The Hermitage names only Holland as the place of creation

when.label: circa 1668
when.note: The Hermitage's record says circa 1668; its Google Arts & Culture entry gives 1663–1665. The range covers both.

journey_fact.text: Bought in Paris for Catherine the Great from the Duc d'Ancezune, it entered the Hermitage in 1766, the museum records (its Google Arts & Culture text says 1767); how it reached France is not documented.

facts.text: The Hermitage says Rembrandt painted this huge canvas without any commission, just months before his death, in a Protestant country where big religious pictures were rare.
It shows the parable in Luke 15: a son who squandered his inheritance kneels before his father, whose red wrap forms a sort of canopy over him.

photo.author: State Hermitage Museum (high-resolution release), via Wikimedia Commons
photo.pd_basis: Painting by Rembrandt (1606–1669), who died more than 70 years ago; faithful photo of a 2D work.

conflicts: Place: the Hermitage names only 'Holland' (Russian record: 'Место создания: Голландия'); Wikidata P1071 and the Commons file give Amsterdam. Country level is used.
Date: the Hermitage record gives circa 1668; the Hermitage's Google Arts & Culture entry gives 1663–1665; Wikidata P571 gives c. 1668 and 1665. The range 1663–1668 covers both museum dates.
Acquisition: the record says it entered the Hermitage in 1766 (collection of Catherine II); the Google Arts & Culture text says acquired in 1767 in Paris from 'Duke d'Ancesuine' (the Duc d'Ancezune).

items.title: Primavera
items.alt_neutral: Wide painting on wood: nine figures cross a flowery meadow in a dark grove of orange trees; at right a blue-skinned winged figure seizes a fleeing nymph beside a woman in a flower-patterned dress; at centre a woman in a red cloak stands beneath a blindfolded flying child aiming an arrow; at left three women in sheer gowns dance in a ring and a young man in red reaches up into the branches
items.caption: Painting of nine figures on a flowery meadow in an orange grove

made.note: First recorded in a Medici house on Via Larga, Florence

when.label: 1480 c. (Uffizi page); 1482-1485 (Uffizi catalogue record)
when.note: The Uffizi page says about 1480 and its catalogue record 1482-1485; any year from 1480 to 1485 scores full marks.

journey_fact.text: Documented in the Medici palace on Via Larga, Florence, from 1498 to 1516; seen by Vasari at the Medici villa of Castello in 1550; in the grand-ducal Guardaroba from 1815, the Accademia from 1853 and the Uffizi since 1919.

facts.text: At least 42 plant species have been identified in it, 14 green plants and 28 flowering ones, all painted accurately, perhaps with the help of herbaria.
It hung above a lettuccio, a chest with a backrest, in the house of the heirs of Lorenzo di Pierfrancesco de' Medici, cousin of Lorenzo the Magnificent.

photo.author: Gallerie degli Uffizi (Google Art Project), via Wikimedia Commons
photo.pd_basis: Sandro Botticelli died 1510; Commons tags the file PD-Art (PD-old-100-expired)
photo.crop_note: Trimmed 1.5% top and bottom and 1.2% at the sides to remove the thin gilt frame strip

conflicts: Date: the Uffizi web page gives '1480 c.'; the Uffizi catalogue record (ICCD 0900158550) gives 1482-1485 and calls the dating controversial (Lightbown suggests 1482); Wikidata Q549847 P571 gives the 1480s with earliest 1480 and latest 1485. The range 1480-1485 covers both museum dates.
Final entry to the Uffizi: the catalogue record says 1919; Wikidata P276 lists Palazzo Medici (1498-1516) and the Uffizi without dates. The museum record is used.

items.title: Apollo Belvedere
items.alt_neutral: Life-size white marble statue of a nude young man with curly hair knotted on top, a cloak slung over his shoulder and draped along his outstretched left arm; his right hand hangs beside a tree stump with a snake coiled up it; sandals on his feet, a strap across his chest and a thin dark support rod behind him, in an arched niche
items.caption: Marble statue of a nude youth with an outstretched arm and cloak

kept.museum: Vatican Museums (Musei Vaticani), Pio Clementino Museum

made.note: A Roman workshop's marble copy of a Greek bronze of about 330 BC

when.label: first decades of the 2nd century A.D.
when.note: The Vatican dates the copy to the first decades of the 2nd century AD; its Greek bronze model dates from about 330 BC.

journey_fact.text: Found in Rome on the Viminal Hill in 1489; entered the Vatican in 1508-1509 for Pope Julius II's Statue Courtyard. Taken to Paris under Napoleon (1798-1815), back in 1816; lent to exhibitions in the United States in 1983.

facts.text: Since its 2020-2024 restoration its left hand is a cast of the 'hand of Baia', a fragment of a Roman-era plaster copy taken from the original Greek statue.
Winckelmann called it 'the highest ideal of art among the ancient works that have been preserved to us so far'.

photo.author: Fabrizio Garrisi, via Wikimedia Commons
photo.pd_basis: Roman marble of the early 2nd century AD; no copyright in the object

conflicts: Find spot: the Vatican says Rome, among the ruins of an ancient domus on the Viminal Hill (1489); Wikidata Q619135 P189 says Anzio. The museum is used.

Date: the Vatican gives only 'first decades of the 2nd century A.D.' (IT 'primi decenni del II secolo d.C.'); 101-140 is our numeric reading of that phrase. Wikidata P571 gives the 120s for the copy (inside the range) and -350 (4th century BCE) for the lost bronze original.
Return from Paris: the Apollo page says the statue returned from Paris in 1816; the 2024 restoration page dates the Napoleonic transfer 1798-1815.

items.title: The Rosetta Stone
items.alt_neutral: Broken slab of dark grey polished stone, taller than wide, with a pinkish vein across its upper left corner; its face is covered edge to edge in three bands of finely carved writing: rows of small pictorial signs at the top, a band of flowing cursive script in the middle and long lines of small capital letters at the bottom
items.caption: Broken dark stone slab carved with three bands of writing

made.note: Found reused in a fort wall at el-Rashid; the museum names no place of making

journey_fact.text: Found by French soldiers in July 1799, built into an old wall at a fort near el-Rashid (Rosetta). Under the Treaty of Alexandria (1801) it passed to the British, reached Portsmouth in February 1802 and was given to the museum by George III.

facts.text: It carries one priestly decree for Ptolemy V three times: 14 lines of hieroglyphs, 32 of Demotic and 54 of Ancient Greek. The Greek gave scholars the key to reading the hieroglyphs.
Fearing bombing in 1917, the museum moved it to a station of the Postal Tube Railway 50 feet below Holborn, where it spent two years: its only break from display since 1802.

photo.author: Hans Hillewaert, via Wikimedia Commons
photo.pd_basis: Stela inscribed in 196 BC; no copyright in the object.

conflicts: Place: the British Museum record has no production place, only the findspot Fort Saint Julien (el-Rashid, Egypt); its blog says the stone had been built into a very old wall there, so made is the country, Egypt, not Rashid. Wikidata has no P1071 (P189 Fort Julien, P495 Ptolemaic Kingdom).

claimant_source.text: Egyptologist and former antiquities minister Zahi Hawass runs a public petition for its return, saying it was removed from Egypt illicitly. The museum says Egypt's government has not formally asked for it.

items.title: Tipu's Tiger
items.alt_neutral: Life-size carved and painted wooden figure of a big cat with dark leaf-shaped stripes lying on top of a man on his back; its jaws close on his neck while he wears a red coat, black hat and black shoes; a brass crank handle sits on the animal's flank and a flowered textile hangs behind
items.caption: Carved wooden striped big cat mauling a man lying on his back

made.note: The museum names Mysore; it stood in Tipu's palace at Srirangapatna

journey_fact.text: Found by East India Company troops in the music room of Tipu Sultan's palace at Srirangapatna after the 1799 siege; shipped to East India House, London, in 1800; transferred to the South Kensington Museum (now the V&A) in 1879.

facts.text: Turning a handle on its side makes bellows inside growl and wail while the man's arm moves; a flap opens onto organ pipes and a keyboard with ivory button keys.
It existed by 1792, when the English military artist James Hunter drew it; his drawing is lost, but an engraving of it was printed in a London book of 1800.

photo.author: Laika ac (Flickr), via Wikimedia Commons
photo.pd_basis: Anonymous work of about 1790; no copyright in the object.
photo.crop_note: Crop t,r,b,l = 0.215,0.04,0.14,0.055 (about 4533 x 2137 px left): removes the wall labels and silver dish below, the gallery and a gun at the sides. A tiny case number '2' above the back and a faint arched-window reflection behind the head remain.

conflicts: Date: the V&A record gives 'ca. 1790' with earliest 1785 and latest 1794 and notes it existed by 1792; the V&A article 'Tipu's Tiger' captions it '1780s or 1790s' and says it was 'Commissioned in the 1790s'. Range kept to the record's 1785-1794; widen to 1780-1799 if the article dates must be covered. Wikidata P571: 1790.

Place: the V&A record names 'Mysore' (no city qualifier; the V&A writes 'Sriringapatna' for the town elsewhere) and its article calls Tipu 'ruler of Mysore', so made is the Kingdom of Mysore (Wikidata Q266923, P625 12.3, 76.65), region precision. Wikidata has no P1071 and no P195 (only P276 V&A).

items.title: The Hay Wain
items.alt_neutral: Oil landscape under a wide sky of grey and white clouds: a horse-drawn wooden cart with two men stands in a shallow river; a brick cottage with red roofs and a tall chimney sits among dense trees at left, a small dog watches from the near bank, and sunlit meadows stretch away at right
items.caption: Painting of a horse-drawn cart crossing a shallow river by a cottage

made.note: Shows Flatford in Suffolk; painted in his London studio

facts.text: It shows the millpond at Flatford on the River Stour, about a mile from Constable's birthplace, but he painted it in his London studio, working from open-air sketches made over several years.
Unsold in London, it went to the dealer John Arrowsmith in 1824 and was shown at the Paris Salon, where it caused a sensation and won Constable a gold medal from King Charles X.

photo.author: The National Gallery, London (via gallerix.ru), via Wikimedia Commons
photo.pd_basis: John Constable died 1837; Commons tags the file PD-Art (PD-old-auto-expired, deathyear 1837)

items.title: Liberty Leading the People (28 July 1830)
items.alt_neutral: Large oil painting: a bare-breasted woman in a yellow dress and red cap strides barefoot over a barricade of beams and bodies, holding a red, white and blue flag high in one hand and a musket with bayonet in the other; a man in a top hat with a gun and a boy with two pistols push forward beside her through smoke; twin square towers rise in the hazy distance at right
items.caption: Painting of a woman raising a flag over a barricade of fallen men

made.note: Painted in the studio Delacroix rented on the quai Voltaire, Paris

when.note: Signed and dated 1830; the Louvre says it was painted between September and December 1830.

journey_fact.text: Bought by the State in 1831 and shown at the Musée du Luxembourg; lent back to Delacroix about 1839 and shown in Lyon in 1848-49; at the Luxembourg again 1863-74, then moved to the Louvre in November 1874.

facts.text: The Louvre calls it the only time Delacroix painted Paris; he had witnessed the uprising of 27-29 July 1830 and began the canvas that September.
Shown at the Salon of 1831, it was bought from the artist that August by the Ministry of Commerce and Public Works for 3,000 francs.

photo.author: Photo: Shonagon (2024, after restoration), via Wikimedia Commons
photo.pd_basis: Delacroix died 1863; Commons tags the file PD-Art (PD-old-auto-expired).

items.title: Sun Stone (Piedra del Sol)
items.alt_neutral: Huge round basalt disc carved in shallow relief: a face with a protruding tongue at the centre, framed by four square panels and rings of small glyphs, pointed rays and two serpents meeting at the bottom; rough uncarved stone at the left edge
items.caption: Huge round carved stone disc with a face at its centre

made.note: Basalt from the south of the basin, set up in Tenochtitlan's Sacred Precinct

when.label: 1250/1500; carved around 1512
when.note: INAH's record gives 1250/1500 (Late Postclassic, ca. 1500); its text says it was carved around 1512.

journey_fact.text: Thrown into the main square after Tenochtitlan fell in 1521 and later buried; found under the Plaza Mayor on 17 December 1790, set against the cathedral tower, moved to the National Museum in 1885 and to this museum in 1964.

facts.text: The museum calls the name "Aztec Calendar" a misnomer: the stone expresses the Mexica idea of time but never worked as a calendar.
It weighs 24.5 tonnes; the museum says it was probably towed 12 to 22 km into Tenochtitlan's Sacred Precinct with ropes, levers, rollers and hundreds of workers.

photo.author: Arian Zwegers, via Wikimedia Commons
photo.pd_basis: Anonymous Mexica stone sculpture of the Late Postclassic period (before 1521); no copyright in the object.
photo.crop_note: Crop bottom 0.06 to remove the plinth, which carries an audio-guide sticker

conflicts: Date: INAH's record gives 1250/1500 and its text 'around the year 1512'; Wikidata P571 gives 1510 (earliest 1502, latest 1520); an INAH journal article (revistas.inah.gob.mx) dates it to 1479 under Axayacatl. The range covers both museum dates.

Place: Wikidata has no P1071; the museum names no carving workshop, only the stone's source (south of the Basin of Mexico) and its first setting (Sacred Precinct of Tenochtitlan), so the record uses the region.

items.title: The warship Vasa
items.alt_neutral: Large wooden sailing warship seen from the side in a dim hall: a dark timber hull with two rows of square gunports, a carved beakhead at the left, three bare masts with rope rigging, and carved galleries at the stern
items.caption: Huge dark wooden warship with three masts and rows of gunports

made.note: Built at Skeppsgården, the navy yard in Stockholm

journey_fact.text: Sank in Stockholm harbour on its maiden voyage in 1628 and lay in the mud for 333 years; raised on 24 April 1961, shown at the temporary Wasa Shipyard from 1962, and in the new Vasa Museum since it opened on 15 June 1990.

facts.text: On 10 August 1628 it heeled over and sank only 1,300 metres into its maiden voyage, still within sight of the yard where it was built.
From 1962 to 1979 the hull was sprayed around the clock with polyethylene glycol from 500 nozzles, so the waterlogged wood would not shrink and crack.

photo.author: Je-str, via Wikimedia Commons
photo.pd_basis: Ship built 1626-1628 by shipwrights of the Swedish crown; no copyright in the object.
photo.crop_note: Crop right 0.135 and bottom 0.13 to remove visitors behind the stern and on the floor; the tip of the stern gallery is lost

items.title: The Liberty Bell
items.alt_neutral: Large dark bronze bell hanging from a heavy weathered wooden yoke between metal posts; two bands of raised lettering run around the shoulder, more lettering sits on the side, and a long dark crack climbs from the rim
items.caption: Large cracked bronze bell hanging from a dark wooden yoke

made.note: Recast in Philadelphia from a London-made bell that cracked

journey_fact.text: Rang in the tower of the Pennsylvania State House, now Independence Hall; from the late 1800s it travelled across the country to expositions and fairs, and it is now shown in the Liberty Bell Center.

facts.text: The wide "crack" is an 1846 repair: workers drilled the thin split wider to stop it spreading, but a second crack then silenced the bell for good.
Abolitionists named it: the Anti-Slavery Record first called it the Liberty Bell in 1835, taking up its inscription "Proclaim Liberty Throughout All the Land".

photo.author: Gage Skidmore, via Wikimedia Commons
photo.pd_basis: Bronze bell cast in 1753 by John Pass and John Stow; no copyright in the object.

items.title: Dancing Girl
items.alt_neutral: Small dark bronze statuette of a slender nude young woman with one hand on her hip; the other arm, ringed with bangles from shoulder to wrist, rests on a bent leg; she wears a necklace of leaf-like pendants and her hair in a heavy bun
items.caption: Small bronze figure of a nude young woman, one hand on her hip

made.note: Excavated at Mohenjo-daro; the museum names no workshop

journey_fact.text: Recovered in excavations in the 'HR area' of Mohenjo-daro, in today's Pakistan; how and when it reached New Delhi is not documented on the museum's page.

facts.text: It is only 10.5 cm tall; the museum notes that her left arm is covered entirely in heavy ringed bangles, quite unlike the right.
The museum calls it one of the rarest artifacts in the world, more supple and sensuous than the heavily ornamented clay figurines of the same culture.

photo.author: Gary Todd, via Wikimedia Commons
photo.pd_basis: Bronze statuette of about 2500 BCE; no copyright in the object.

conflicts: Place: the museum names only 'Mohenjodaro' and says the statue was recovered in excavation from the 'HR area'; Wikidata has find locations (P189) Mohenjo-daro and Sindh and no P1071, so Made is the region.

claimant_source.text: In November 2016 lawyer Abdul Wahab Baloch petitioned the Sindh High Court to declare that the statuette belongs to Sindh and to seek its return from India, directly or through UNESCO.

items.title: Gold funerary mask (the "Mask of Agamemnon")
items.alt_neutral: Thin hammered gold mask of a man's face with closed eyes, arched brows, a long narrow nose, a curled moustache and a beard drawn in fine lines; the ears stand out at the sides and the edges are torn and creased
items.caption: Hammered gold mask of a bearded man's face with closed eyes

made.note: Found in Grave Circle A at Mycenae; the museum names no workshop

when.label: 16th century BC
when.note: The museum dates the Grave Circle A rulers to the 16th century BC.

journey_fact.text: Dug up in 1876 in Grave Circle A at Mycenae by Heinrich Schliemann, supervised by the ephor Panagiotis Stamatakis; the finds were first shown at the Polytechnic in Athens in October 1877, later in the museum's Mycenaean Gallery.

facts.text: Schliemann linked the mask to Homer's King Agamemnon, but the museum says the Circle A rulers lived in the 16th century BC, at least four centuries before the Trojan War.
The ephor Panagiotis Stamatakis recorded every object where it lay; the museum credits his diary with correcting several of Schliemann's exaggerations.

photo.author: Jebulon, via Wikimedia Commons
photo.pd_basis: Mycenaean gold mask of the 16th century BC; no copyright in the object.

conflicts: Date: the museum gives the 16th century BC; Wikidata P571 has two values, 1600 BCE (century) and 1550 BCE (earliest 1550, latest 1500 BCE). The museum's century is used.
Place: Wikidata has find location (P189) Mycenae and no P1071; the museum names only the find spot, so Made is the region.

items.title: Self-Portrait with Fur-Trimmed Robe
items.alt_neutral: Oil portrait on wood of a young man facing straight out against a black ground, long curling reddish-brown hair to his shoulders, a short beard, a brown coat with a fur collar and one hand raised to the collar; gold lettering and a monogram on the dark ground at both sides
items.caption: Painting of a long-haired man facing out, in a fur-collared coat

made.note: Signed 'Albrecht Dürer of Nuremberg'; bought from Nuremberg in 1805

journey_fact.text: Bought from Nuremberg for the Bavarian state collection in 1805, the museum records; its earlier history is not documented on the museum's page.

facts.text: Its Latin inscription reads: "I, Albrecht Dürer of Nuremberg portrayed myself in appropriate colours aged twenty-eight years."
The museum says Dürer based this strictly frontal pose on icons of Christ the Saviour, with the hand raised as in a blessing.

photo.author: Bayerische Staatsgemäldesammlungen – Alte Pinakothek, via Wikimedia Commons
photo.pd_basis: Albrecht Dürer died in 1528; Commons tags PD-Art (PD-old-100-expired).

items.title: Venus of Willendorf
items.alt_neutral: Small rounded limestone figure of a nude woman with heavy breasts, a wide belly with a deep navel and full hips; thin arms rest on the breasts, the head is covered in rows of knob-like braids with no face shown, and the legs end at the knees
items.caption: Small stone figure of a rounded woman, her head covered in braids

kept.museum: Natural History Museum Vienna (Naturhistorisches Museum Wien)

made.note: Found at Willendorf in the Wachau; the museum names no place of carving

when.label: Paleolithic Age, 29,500 years
when.note: The museum gives an age of 29,500 years; stored as about 27,500 BCE.

journey_fact.text: Found in August 1908 at Willendorf in the Wachau during an excavation by the Natural History Museum Vienna, which has kept it since.

facts.text: It was carved from fine limestone with flint tools and was originally coated with red chalk, a colour the museum links with life, death and rebirth.
It has no facial features; the museum reads this as a universal figure rather than a portrait of one woman.

photo.author: Bjørn Christian Tørrissen, via Wikimedia Commons
photo.pd_basis: Palaeolithic stone figure about 29,500 years old; no copyright in the object.
photo.crop_note: The file shows four views side by side; crop right 0.75 to keep only the front view (about 2427 x 4573)

conflicts: Place: Wikidata has find location (P189) Willendorf II and discovery date (P575) 7 August 1908 but no P1071 or P571; the museum names only the find spot, so Made is the region.

items.title: Muisca Raft (Balsa Muisca)
items.alt_neutral: Small cast-gold model of a flat oval raft made of woven bars, carrying a tall central figure with a large headdress and ear ornaments, surrounded by smaller figures holding staffs and banners
items.caption: Gold model of a raft carrying a large central figure and attendants

kept.museum: Museo del Oro, Banco de la República

made.note: Found in a cave at Pasca, Cundinamarca; the museum names no workshop

journey_fact.text: Found in 1969 in a cave on La Campana hill at Pasca, Cundinamarca, by Cruz María Dimaté and a son; the parish priest contacted Banco de la República, which acquired it that year for the Gold Museum.

facts.text: A similar gold raft found in Lake Siecha in 1856 was sold to a museum in Germany and lost in a fire when its ship reached Bremen.
It was made to be offered, not worn: the bank says it was left with other offerings in a cave on the southern edge of Muisca territory.

photo.author: Pedro Szekely, via Wikimedia Commons
photo.pd_basis: Pre-Hispanic Muisca goldwork, 600-1600 CE; no copyright in the object.

conflicts: Date: the museum's encyclopedia gives the late Muisca period, 600-1600 CE; Wikidata P571 gives 1600 (year precision).
Place: Wikidata has no P1071 or find location; the museum names only the find spot (Pasca, Cundinamarca), so Made is the region.

items.title: 1903 Wright Flyer
items.alt_neutral: Fragile biplane of wooden struts, wire bracing and pale cream fabric, seen from the front quarter on black: long double wings, a small double elevator at the front, two slender propellers behind the wings and a tall twin rudder at the back
items.caption: Early biplane of wood and pale fabric with two long propellers

kept.museum: National Air and Space Museum (Smithsonian Institution)

made.note: Built in the Wrights' Dayton shop; assembled and flown at Kitty Hawk

journey_fact.text: Wrecked by a gust after its fourth flight in 1903, it went back to Dayton and sat in storage, flooded in 1913; lent to London's Science Museum in 1928, it returned in 1948 and was given to the Smithsonian that December.

facts.text: Its first flight, at Kitty Hawk on 17 December 1903 with Orville at the controls, lasted 12 seconds and covered 36 m (120 ft).
The fabric is not the 1903 cloth: it was re-covered for the London loan in 1927 and again in 1985, using surviving flown wing fabric as a pattern.

photo.author: National Air and Space Museum, Smithsonian Institution
photo.pd_basis: Aircraft built in 1903 by Wilbur and Orville Wright; a functional machine with no surviving copyright.

items.title: Narmer Palette
items.alt_neutral: Shield-shaped dark stone slab carved in low relief: two cow-horned faces at the top flank a small framed sign; below, a tall crowned figure raises a mace over a kneeling captive, a falcon perches above, and two fallen men fill the bottom band
items.caption: Carved stone slab: a crowned figure raises a mace over a captive

made.note: Found at Hierakonpolis (Kom al-Ahmar) near Edfu; no workshop named

when.label: beginning of the First Dynasty (c. 3100 BC)

journey_fact.text: Discovered in the remains of an Old Kingdom temple complex at Hierakonpolis, near Edfu in Upper Egypt; how and when it reached the Egyptian Museum in Cairo is not documented on the ministry's page.

facts.text: Egypt's antiquities ministry calls this green schist palette one of the crown jewels of the Egyptian Museum, from the dawn of Egyptian civilization.

photo.author: Archivio fotografico Museo Egizio, Turin (early 20th-century postcard), via Wikimedia Commons
photo.pd_basis: Carved stone palette of about 3100 BC; no copyright in the object.
photo.crop_note: Crop top 0.05, right 0.05, bottom 0.12, left 0.05 to remove the postcard margin and its printed caption ('Palette of the King Narmer ... Cairo Museum', no. 778)

conflicts: Date: the ministry gives c. 3100 BC; Wikidata P571 gives the 31st century BCE (earliest 3100, latest 3000 BCE).
Place: Wikidata has find location (P189) Temple of Hierakonpolis and no P1071; the ministry names only the find spot, so Made is the region.

items.title: Terrace of a Café at Night (Place du Forum)
items.alt_neutral: Oil painting at night: lamplit outdoor tables under a yellow awning, figures seated and strolling, dark blue houses and a star-filled sky over a cobbled square
items.caption: Night scene: lamplit outdoor tables under a yellow awning, starry sky

made.note: Painted on the spot, after dark, on a square in Arles

journey_fact.text: Painted in Arles in September 1888. The collector Helene Kröller-Müller bought it (when is not documented in the museum's texts); her foundation gave the collection to the Dutch State in 1935, and the Otterlo museum opened in 1938.

facts.text: Van Gogh painted the gaslit terrace on the spot and in the dark; astronomers later found that its stars match the sky of 16 or 17 September 1888.
He wanted a night painting without black and grey; he wrote that gaslight, being yellow and orange, "intensifies blue".

photo.author: Kröller-Müller Museum, via Wikimedia Commons
photo.pd_basis: Vincent van Gogh died in 1890; a faithful reproduction of a public-domain painting.

items.title: David
items.alt_neutral: Colossal white stone statue of a nude young man with curly hair, weight on one leg, head turned to his left, a sling over his shoulder and a tree stump beside his leg
items.caption: Colossal stone nude: a young man with a sling over his shoulder

made.note: Commissioned by the works of Florence cathedral; unveiled in Florence in 1504

journey_fact.text: Stood at the entrance of Palazzo Vecchio from 1504; moved from Piazza della Signoria in August 1873 and waited nine years in a wooden box until its tribune at the Galleria dell'Accademia was built.

facts.text: Florence cathedral's works gave Michelangelo the commission on 16 August 1501 for 400 ducats; the statue was unveiled to the city on 8 September 1504.
Parts of it were once gilded: a garland on the head, the tree stump behind the right leg and the sling. With its carved base it is 517 cm high and weighs 5,560 kg.

photo.author: Jörg Bittner Unna, via Wikimedia Commons
photo.pd_basis: Marble statue carved 1501-1504 by Michelangelo (died 1564); no copyright in the work.

items.title: Apollo and Daphne
items.alt_neutral: White stone group: a running young man reaches for a fleeing young woman whose fingers and hair are turning into leaves and whose feet are turning into roots
items.caption: Stone group: a running youth grasps a woman turning into a tree

made.note: Carved for Cardinal Scipione Borghese's villa in Rome, where it still stands

journey_fact.text: Placed in 1625 in Room 3 of Cardinal Scipione Borghese's villa, as Bernini wished, and still there; the Italian state bought the Borghese collection in 1902.

facts.text: Payment records follow the whole job: the marble block was bought on 2 August 1622 and Bernini received his last payment on 24 November 1625, 1,000 scudi in all.
For Apollo, Bernini copied one of the most famous ancient statues, the Apollo Belvedere, down to the god's sandals.

photo.author: Architas, via Wikimedia Commons
photo.pd_basis: Marble group carved 1622-1625 by Gian Lorenzo Bernini (died 1680); no copyright in the work.
photo.crop_note: Bottom 8.5% cut away (--crop 0,0,0.085,0): removes the modern pedestal and the painted inventory letters 'CV' on the base

items.title: Impression, Sunrise
items.alt_neutral: Loose oil sketch of a misty harbour at dawn in blue-grey and green: a small orange sun and its broken reflection, a dark rowing boat with standing figures, cranes and masts in the haze
items.caption: Misty harbour at dawn: a small orange sun over water and rowing boats

made.note: Painted from a hotel window over the harbour at Le Havre

journey_fact.text: Painted in Le Havre in 1872 and shown in Paris in 1874 at the first exhibition of the group soon called Impressionists; Eugène and Victorine Donop de Monchy gave it to the Musée Marmottan, which received it on 23 May 1940.

facts.text: It gave Impressionism its name: a critic mocked the title in his review "L'exposition des impressionnistes" on 25 April 1874.
Painted in just a few hours; the rowing boats and the bright orange sun with its reflection were added last.

photo.author: Unknown photographer (art database scan), via Wikimedia Commons
photo.pd_basis: Claude Monet died in 1926; a faithful reproduction of a public-domain painting.

items.title: Irises
items.alt_neutral: Oil painting of a garden bed crowded with blue-violet flowers on twisting stems and sword-shaped green leaves, one white flower at left, orange blooms behind and red-brown earth in front
items.caption: Garden bed of blue-violet flowers and sword-shaped leaves, one white

made.note: Painted from nature in the garden of the asylum at Saint-Rémy

journey_fact.text: Painted at Saint-Rémy in May 1889; the critic Octave Mirbeau bought it in 1891. Sold at Sotheby's New York in 1987 to Alan Bond, it went back to Sotheby's in 1990, which sold it privately to the Getty.

facts.text: Van Gogh began it within his first week at the Saint-Rémy asylum, working from nature in its garden; he called it a study.
His brother Theo sent it to the Salon des Indépendants in September 1889 and wrote that it "strikes the eye from afar".

photo.author: J. Paul Getty Museum (Open Content Program)
photo.pd_basis: Vincent van Gogh died in 1890; the Getty marks the work 'No Copyright'.

items.title: Paris Street; Rainy Day
items.alt_neutral: Large oil painting of a wet cobbled crossroads: a couple in dark clothes under one umbrella walk toward the viewer, a green lamppost splits the scene, pale stone apartment blocks behind
items.caption: Wet cobbled crossroads: a couple under an umbrella, a green lamppost

made.note: Shows an intersection a short walk from the artist's Paris home

journey_fact.text: Stayed with the artist's family after his death in 1894; sold to the collector Walter P. Chrysler Jr., New York, in 1954, then to Wildenstein and Company, which sold it to the Art Institute in 1964.

facts.text: Caillebotte's largest and most ambitious painting, over two metres high; he showed it at the third Impressionist exhibition in 1877.
Rain is never painted as drops: it shows in the new retractable umbrellas and the reflections on the wet cobblestones.

photo.author: Art Institute of Chicago
